LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Fifteen Mangoes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson counts fifteen the efficient way: three rows of five. Your child counts fifteen mangoes row by row, says the ten-and-five recipe and learns that counting by fives is the first counting shortcut.

What is this?

Fifteen is ten and five more — fifteen mangoes in three rows of five. It is also the halfway house of the teens, and the first number that begs to be counted in fives instead of ones.

What does it mean?

Counting by ones to fifteen is a long walk; counting by rows is a shortcut. Three fives make fifteen, and that insight — equal groups make big numbers — is the doorway to skip counting and, much later, multiplication.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three fifteens: the ten-and-five recipe; row counting — five, five, five; and the halfway feeling: fifteen is exactly midway between ten and twenty.

Why this matters

Fives are the friendliest grouping for young counters — they match hands. A child who counts fifteen as three rows of five is doing real structural math with fruit, and the halfway landmark gives the teens a middle they can aim at.

What it teaches

Skip counting by fives (seeds of it), equal-groups reading, halfway landmarks on the number line, and the ten-plus-five recipe — one more teen number absorbed into the pattern.

Words to learn

fifteenhalfwayrows of fiveshortcutten and fivemiddle

Say this to your child

“"Fifteen mangoes — ten and five more, or three rows of five. Fifteen is the middle of the teens, halfway from ten to twenty. Counting by rows is the counting shortcut."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Fifteen mangoes in three rows of five. We could count one by one... or we could take the shortcut."
  2. Count the slow way once: all fifteen, one touch per mango. Respect the long walk.
  3. Take the shortcut: count each row — five, five, five. Then count all: fifteen. Same answer, half the breath.
  4. Say the recipe: ten and five more. Count a full ten, then the last row of five — fifteen.
  5. Find the middle: "Fifteen is exactly halfway between ten and twenty." Hop three times: ten, fifteen, twenty — short hop, big landmark.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 15 stands over fifteen smiling yellow mangoes with leaves, arranged in three rows of five, and the word "mangoes" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many mangoes? How many rows and how many in each?" "What is ten and five more?" "What number is halfway between ten and twenty?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Five, five, five — fifteen!" "Ten and five!" or the landmark claim: "Fifteen is the middle one."

Out in the real world

Fifteens tick in quiet places: fifteen minutes is a quarter of an hour (the kitchen timer proves it), fifteen items in a long shop list, fifteen steps to the letterbox. The timer is the star — one ding per quarter hour all afternoon.

Try it together

Row builder: deal fifteen snacks into three rows of five exactly like the card, count by rows, then eat a row and count what remains — ten! Two rows of five are just ten wearing a snack outfit. Then hop the landmark: jump from ten to fifteen to twenty, shouting the landings.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many mangoes? What are the rows? What is the recipe?" Fifteen, three rows of five, ten and five — the halfway number is claimed.

Parent tips

Let them count by ones first — the shortcut only feels like a shortcut after the long walk. If a row gets sixteen, count again together and shrug; the rows make errors easy to see and easy to fix, which is why they are here.

This lesson pairs with the Fifteen Mangoes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).
